newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan still undecided on liquor tax revisions -MOF.
newsitem.headline: Japan still undecided on liquor tax revisions -MOF.

text.p: Japan has made no decision yet on a possible revision of its liquor tax following a ruling by the World Trade Organisation (WTO) that its duties on spirits break international trade rules, Finance Minister Wataru Kubo said on Friday.

The World Trade Organisation (WTO), ruling on a complaint by the European Union, the United States and Canada, has found that Japan taxes imported spirits unfairly compared with a domestic liquor known as shochu.
Although there are still steps to take in formalising the WTO decision, the ruling is unlikely to be changed, Kubo said.
"There are various ways of coping with the WTO decision, such as lowering taxes on whiskey, raising taxes on shochu, or a mixture of the two," he said.
"We have yet to decide which options to take," he added.

Separately, bilateral talks with the United States to meet a self-imposed December 15 deadline to resolve the issue of Japan's insurance industry are not likely to resume until after the U.S. presidential elections on November 5, Kubo told a regular news conference.

"Resuming full-scale negotiations (on insurance) toward the December 15 (deadline) would likely be sometime after November 5," Kubo said. He added that there were no discrepancies between the two nations over an agreement forged earlier to bar Japanese insurers' subsidiaries from selling some products in the niche "third-sector" market before January 1.

Kubo said that starting on January 1, Japanese firms will be allowed to sell all products in the niche market, in which foreign firms have a strong presence, even if the dispute with the United States is not solved by the deadline.
However, these conditions could be revised if the two countries agree to change them, he added.

Kubo was responding to a question about media reports which said U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said on Thursday that Washington will retaliate if Japan lets insurance units enter the niche market without any bilateral agreement.

Meanwhile, Kubo reiterated his view that a planned consumption tax hike to five percent from the current three percent on April 1, 1997 should be carried out as scheduled to make up for fund shortfalls stemming from previous tax cuts.
However, he stressed that structural flaws in the consumption tax should be reviewed in light of overall reforms in Japan's tax system after the elections, which are scheduled for October 20.
